To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the genetic architecture of Parkinson’s disease is more complex than previously thought and that the identification of additional genetic factors will provide insight into the etiology of this disorder.

1) genome-wide association study approaches have identified 21 loci associated to sporadic Parkinson’s Disease, 2) these loci harbor variants with a cumulative risk estimate of 1.4% (95% CI: 1.1-1.8%), 3) the identified genes and variants are involved in biological pathways relevant to PD, and 4) additional studies are needed to identify the functional causal variant(s) in the associated regions.
genome-wide association studies have identified ~20 susceptibility loci for Parkinson’s disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the genes and genetic variation that contribute to the risk of developing PD.
understanding the genetic etiology of sporadic PD.
identifying the genetic factors that contribute to Parkinson’s disease risk and the biological pathways in which they operate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the genetic architecture of sporadic Parkinson’s Disease is complex and that a combination of genetic and environmental factors are likely to play a role in its etiology.
the genetic basis of PD is still largely unknown and that further studies are necessary to fully understand the disease.
genetic studies are a powerful tool for the identification of susceptibility loci in PD and that the identification of the variants driving risk will provide new insights into disease etiology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic association studies have been successful in identifying common variants that contribute to the etiology of PD.
we have identified 21 loci for PD.

GWAS have identified 21 loci associated to sporadic Parkinson’s Disease and that additional studies are necessary to understand the functional variants that are driving disease risk and to identify novel loci.
The main takeaway from our work is that
genetic studies have been very successful at identifying new susceptibility genes and variants for PD.
genetic association studies are a useful tool for the identification of disease risk loci.
the genetic architecture of sporadic PD appears to be complex, and the identification of all the genes involved in disease risk will be a challenge.
